body_text:
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part I (Differentiation of Integrals).
Let $f : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous, and define the area accumulator
function $F : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ by:
$$ F(x) = \int_a^x f(t) \, dt. $$
Then $F$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable on $(a, b)$, and its
derivative satisfies:
$$ F'(x) = f(x) \quad \text{for all } x \in (a, b). $$

*Proof*: For $x \in (a, b)$ and non-zero displacement $h$ such that $x + h \in [a, b]$:
$$ \frac{F(x + h) - F(x)}{h} - f(x) = \frac{1}{h} \int_x^{x+h} f(t) \, dt - \frac{1}{h} \int_x^{x+h} f(x) \, dt = \frac{1}{h} \int_x^{x+h} (f(t) - f(x)) \, dt. $$
Let $\epsilon > 0$. By continuity of $f$ at $x$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that
$|t - x| < \delta \implies |f(t) - f(x)| < \epsilon$.
Then for any $0 < |h| < \delta$:
$$ \left| \frac{F(x + h) - F(x)}{h} - f(x) \right| \leq \frac{1}{|h|} \left| \int_x^{x+h} |f(t) - f(x)| \, dt \right| \leq \frac{1}{|h|} \cdot |h| \epsilon = \epsilon. $$
Taking the limit as $h \to 0$ proves $F'(x) = f(x)$.
